title: Find Minimum Time to Finish All Jobs
statement:
You are given the durations of `n` jobs, `jobs[i]`, and `k` workers. Every job must be assigned to **exactly one** worker, and a worker may receive any number of jobs (possibly none). A worker's **working time** is the sum of the durations of the jobs assigned to them.

Assign the jobs so that the **maximum working time over all workers** is as small as possible, and print that minimum value.

Be careful with greedy strategies such as repeatedly giving the next largest job to the currently least loaded worker: they are fast but not always optimal (see the third example).
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers `jobs[0] ... jobs[n-1]`.
The third line contains an integer `k`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the smallest possible maximum working time.

examples.explanation: With one worker per job, the longest job (3) is the maximum working time, and no assignment can do better than the longest single job.
Give one worker the jobs 1, 2 and 8 (total 11) and the other the jobs 4 and 7 (total 11). The total is 22, so 11 is the best possible split.
Giving 5 and 5 to one worker (10) and 4, 4, 4 to the other (12) gives 12. An 11/11 split is impossible because no subset sums to 11, and a largest-job-first greedy ends up with 13 for one worker.

hints: The answer lies between max(jobs) and sum(jobs), and if a limit T is achievable then any larger limit is too, so you can binary search on T.
For a fixed T the question becomes: can the jobs be packed into at most k groups, each of total at most T? With n ≤ 12 you can track subsets of jobs as bitmasks.

Let dp[mask] be the pair (groups used, load of the last group) minimised lexicographically over all ways to place the jobs in mask. Add one job at a time: either it fits in the last group, or it opens a new one. Alternatively, a backtracking search with pruning (skip workers with equal loads, stop when the load exceeds the best known) also works.
